title: PromptForge x Redwood - cost transparency / unit economics discovery
summary: PromptForge is evaluating Redwood for production inference for a multi-tenant SaaS “prompt management + agent workflows” product. Their key blocker is cost transparency: they need to attribute inference spend by model and region (and eventually plan/tier) to price their own SKUs and to answer customer questions (esp. EU customers). They asked specifically for a metric they can track over time like “$/1M output tokens” with drilldowns and a way to reconcile it with invoices/cloud spend. Redwood (Felix/Allison) explained current metering (input/output tokens, streaming caveats, routing/region metadata), how Redwood thinks about blended vs marginal cost, and what we can provide short-term (exports, per-request metering + dimensions) vs what’s on the roadmap. PromptForge also asked about caching/batching knobs and whether Redwood can show cache hit rate / batching utilization alongside unit cost so they can understand variance. Call ended with an agreement to share a sample cost breakdown by model/region, confirm required dimensions (region normalization, model versions, quantization profile), and schedule a deeper technical session focused on their traffic patterns and EU deployment needs.
topics: Why PromptForge needs cost transparency (pricing, margin tracking, customer reporting)
Target metric: blended $/1M output tokens and reconciliation expectations
Required dimensions: model, model version, quantization profile, region, streaming flag, customer tier
Traffic pattern details: burstiness, long-context usage, streaming usage
Latency vs cost tradeoffs; batching and caching; why unit costs can shift week to week
EU residency and region selection; need for region-level reporting
Short-term reporting options vs internal dashboard roadmap
questions: Can Redwood provide cost per output token by model and by region (weekly/monthly) and reconcile it to billed spend?
If we use streaming, are output tokens metered identically vs non-streaming?
Can you break out cost differences by model version / quant profile (e.g., fp16 vs int8) so we can track optimization experiments?
Do you expose cache hit rate / batching efficiency so we can explain cost swings?
How do you treat idle capacity / overhead in “blended” costs, especially for dedicated capacity?
next_steps: Redwood (Felix) to send a sample report format for $/1M output tokens with drilldowns by model + region (even if manual/export-based initially).
PromptForge (Jon) to share approximate request distribution: context length histogram, output length, % streaming, and peak QPS by region.
Redwood (Allison) to confirm what telemetry dimensions are available today (region, model id/version, streaming flag) and any known gaps.
Schedule a 60-min technical deep dive the following week to review batching/caching behavior and region routing options (EU focus).
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-01-17
Start time: 10:02 AM PT
Duration: ~44 min
Title: PromptForge x Redwood - cost transparency / unit economics discovery
Attendees:
- Felix Schneider (Redwood Inference)
- Allison Grant (Redwood Inference)
- Maya Patel (PromptForge)
- Jon Kim (PromptForge)
- Elena Rios (PromptForge)

Auto-Summary (Fireflies)
- Customer wants cost transparency by model + region for pricing and margin.
- Discussion of unit cost metric and the need to reconcile vs billing.
- Discussed streaming token metering and cost variability drivers (caching/batching/quantization).
- Next steps: sample report + traffic distribution + technical follow-up.

Topics
1) Introductions + current state
2) What “cost transparency” means to PromptForge
3) Desired metrics and dimensions
4) Region/EU requirements
5) Next steps

Action Items
- Felix to share example cost breakdown by model/region and define “blended $/1M output tokens” at a high level.
- Jon to send traffic profile details (context/output lengths, streaming, peak QPS, regions).
- Allison to confirm telemetry dimension availability and any streaming parity caveats.

Transcript

[00:00] Felix Schneider: Cool, hey everyone. Thanks for jumping on. I’m Felix, I work with the solutions side at Redwood. Allison is here as well, she runs a lot of our observability stuff.

[00:10] Allison Grant: Hey all.

[00:12] Maya Patel: Hi, I’m Maya, product. Thanks for making time.

[00:16] Jon Kim: Hey, Jon here, ML eng.

[00:18] Elena Rios: Hi, Elena, finance ops. I’m mostly here to understand how we can report costs.

[00:24] Felix Schneider: Great. So this one is meant to be discovery, right? You all reached out about “cost transparency” specifically. Before we jump into the weeds, can you give us the quick background: what PromptForge is doing with models today, and what problems you’re trying to solve?

[00:38] Maya Patel: Yeah. PromptForge is basically a workflow builder for prompts and agents. Multi-tenant SaaS. Our customers build automations that call LLMs, sometimes chat style, sometimes extraction, sometimes like classification.

[00:54] Maya Patel: We currently use mostly OpenAI for the bread-and-butter, and we have some Anthropic for longer context stuff. But the big issue is we’re getting squeezed on margin and we can’t actually explain cost. Like, our enterprise customers ask “why is EU more expensive” or “why did this week spike” and we don’t have a clean answer.

[01:12] Elena Rios: Yeah and internally, for pricing, we’re trying to move to a usage-based plan, but we need to understand cost per unit. We keep saying “tokens” but it’s messy. Different models, different regions, sometimes streaming.

[01:26] Felix Schneider: Makes sense. When you say “explain cost,” do you mean per customer, per workspace, per model, per region, all of the above?

[01:36] Maya Patel: Ultimately per customer and per plan, but the immediate need is by model and region. Because we’re getting asked for EU reporting a lot.

[01:45] Jon Kim: And also like, if we switch from one model variant to another, we want to know the unit cost shift. Not just invoice surprises at the end.

[01:55] Felix Schneider: Got it. And right now, are you routing by region? Like do you run EU in EU, or do you just hit a single endpoint and hope for the best.

[02:03] Jon Kim: OpenAI is kind of opaque there. We do some region pinning in our app layer for EU customers when possible but it’s not consistent. We’ve tested Together AI for open models but we didn’t like the variance.

[02:18] Felix Schneider: Okay. So let’s anchor on what you want as an output. Elena, if you had the perfect dashboard or report, what would it show? Like, what’s the metric.

[02:29] Elena Rios: The simplest thing is something like blended dollars per one million output tokens. And then I want to filter by model and region. If it’s “gpt-4o-mini” vs “llama 3.1 70b” or whatever, and “us-east” vs “eu-west”, what’s the actual cost per 1M tokens. And it needs to reconcile to spend.

[02:52] Felix Schneider: “Output tokens” specifically, not total tokens.

[02:55] Elena Rios: Output is what drives user value. But we probably want both. Output is what we price on.

[03:02] Maya Patel: And to be honest, we don’t care if it’s perfect down to the penny, but we need something trustworthy enough for exec reviews.

[03:10] Allison Grant: When you say reconcile, do you mean reconcile to your vendor bill, or reconcile to cloud GPU spend, or both?

[03:17] Elena Rios: Vendor bill. Like, if we say in January “we spent 120k on inference,” the token-based derived number should tie out or at least have a clear explanation for the delta.

[03:30] Felix Schneider: Yup. So I’ll describe how we typically break it down, then we can talk about feasibility and what we can expose.

[03:38] Felix Schneider: In general, the clean metric is cost / output tokens, but you have to decide: is it marginal cost (like compute used on requests) or blended (compute + idle + overhead allocation). For hosted API we can usually get close to marginal. For dedicated capacity, blended gets tricky because you’ve reserved GPUs and you might be underutilizing.

[03:59] Elena Rios: That makes sense. We’re starting hosted, but we might do dedicated for our largest customer.

[04:05] Maya Patel: Yeah we have one bank prospect who basically said “dedicated or no deal.”

[04:09] Felix Schneider: Understood. Another dimension that matters a lot is region normalization. Everybody uses different region strings. Like “eu-west-1” vs “europe-west” and sometimes internal colos. We normalize that on our side so you can group reliably.

[04:24] Jon Kim: Okay, so you can give us region as a tag. That’s important.

[04:28] Allison Grant: We can, with some caveats. For example, in some paths the “region” you think of is the serving region, but you might also care about “customer selected region” vs “actual served region” if there’s failover.

[04:42] Maya Patel: Yeah that’s actually one of the reasons we want this. If you fail us over to the US, we need to know because of EU commitments.

[04:50] Felix Schneider: Right. We can talk about residency separately, but for cost reporting, we’d ideally store the “served region” as a dimension.

[04:58] Jon Kim: And by model, do you mean like base model name, or actual version? Because we’ve seen vendors switch versions under the hood.

[05:08] Felix Schneider: Great question. We distinguish model identifier and version. For open models, it’s usually explicit. For some managed catalogs, we still try to pin a version. We also have quantization profiles as a separate dimension, since that changes cost and sometimes quality.

[05:24] Jon Kim: That’s exactly what we need. We ran some int8 tests and the savings were real, but we had subtle quality issues.

[05:32] Maya Patel: Our support team also needs to answer “why did this output change.” So having the ability to see quantization changes would be helpful.

[05:40] Felix Schneider: Makes sense.

[05:42] Allison Grant: Quick check: what percent of your traffic is streaming today?

[05:47] Jon Kim: Probably 70% streaming for chat experiences. Non-streaming for like extraction tasks.

[05:54] Allison Grant: Okay. I’m asking because streaming token accounting can be a footgun across providers. Like, depending on whether you count tokens emitted per chunk or at the end. We do output token metering, but I want to confirm what you need and how strict.

[06:10] Elena Rios: We need it consistent. If streaming is undercounted, then our dollars per token looks worse for non-streaming and it becomes useless.

[06:18] Felix Schneider: Yeah, that’s fair. Internally we treat “token metering parity” as a requirement: streaming and non-streaming should roll up the same. If there’s a gap, it can create fake regressions.

[06:33] Maya Patel: So do you have that parity today?

[06:36] Allison Grant: Mostly, but I’m not going to hand-wave. There are edge cases in the ecosystem—tool calls, truncation, partial completions. What we do is instrument at the runtime layer and also compare to gateway counts. If you want, we can share what dimensions we expose and what we recommend for validation.

[06:56] Jon Kim: That’s good. Another question: you mentioned blended vs marginal. For our use case, we want something stable over time. If you change how you allocate overhead, it’ll break our reporting.

[07:09] Felix Schneider: Totally. If we provide a blended metric, we version it. Like “methodology v1” and it stays consistent. When the cost rate card changes or the allocation model changes, you can see that version and understand step changes.

[07:25] Elena Rios: Rate card meaning GPU hourly cost by region?

[07:28] Felix Schneider: Yeah. Under the hood, you’ve got different GPU costs in eu-west vs us-east, reserved vs on-demand, and so on.

[07:38] Elena Rios: That’s what I care about. We got hit with a big EU delta and nobody could explain if it was actual infra cost or just pricing.

[07:47] Maya Patel: And customers ask us for “EU discount” basically. Like, why is it 1.3x.

[07:53] Felix Schneider: Sure. Another driver we see is batching and caching efficiency. If your traffic is bursty, batching helps, and if prompts share prefixes, caching helps. That can cut cost per output token. But it also makes the metric move around.

[08:10] Jon Kim: Do you expose cache hit rate?

[08:13] Allison Grant: We can expose cache hit rate as a signal, yes, though there are multiple caches (prefix, KV cache reuse, etc.). People say “cache” and mean different things. But the gist is: you want “cache hit rate” and “batching utilization” alongside unit cost, so when cost changes you can say “oh, cache dropped” or “batch size fell.”

[08:35] Jon Kim: Exactly. Because otherwise we chase ghosts.

[08:38] Maya Patel: If the metric is just “$/1M tokens” without explanation, we’ll get internal blame games.

[08:45] Felix Schneider: Yep.

[08:47] Felix Schneider: Can you share a bit on traffic patterns? Like, context lengths and output lengths. Long context can change prefill vs decode cost.

[08:56] Jon Kim: We have two big modes. One is chat: context maybe 4k to 12k tokens, output 200-800. The other is “doc summarize + extraction” where context can be 50k sometimes, output like 500-1.5k.

[09:14] Allison Grant: 50k context, okay. That tends to make prefill cost dominate. So if you price on output tokens only, the unit economics can look weird.

[09:25] Elena Rios: That’s a really good point. We’ve been debating pricing on output tokens but then we have these “long input” workloads.

[09:33] Maya Patel: But customers hate paying for input because they don’t understand it.

[09:37] Felix Schneider: Yeah, common problem. Some folks do “input + output” but weight them, or do “compute units.” But if your stated goal is blended $/1M output tokens, we can still compute it; you just need to interpret it carefully for long-context requests.

[09:55] Jon Kim: In other words, we’ll see higher $/output token when inputs are huge.

[09:58] Allison Grant: Exactly.

[10:00] Felix Schneider: On the region part, do you need EU data residency guarantees, or just prefer EU latency.

[10:08] Maya Patel: For some customers, actual residency. Nordic bank prospect. They said “must stay in EU.” We also have healthcare customers in the US, but that’s easier.

[10:19] Felix Schneider: Okay. So in that case, region reporting needs to align with enforcement. Like, if you say EU-only and we fail over, that should be visible and ideally not allowed unless you opt in.

[10:32] Jon Kim: Right.

[10:34] Felix Schneider: I know this call is about cost transparency, but it’s related. Because for a lot of teams, the first time they notice failover is when cost spikes in a different region.

[10:43] Elena Rios: Exactly.

[10:45] Allison Grant: Another question: do you need model-level cost for multiple model vendors, or just if you use Redwood as the inference provider.

[10:54] Maya Patel: For now, just within Redwood. If we move traffic onto Redwood, we need that cost report. Cross-vendor would be nice but we can stitch separately.

[11:04] Felix Schneider: Cool.

[11:06] Jon Kim: Can I ask something blunt: do you have an actual dashboard for this? Or is it like “we can send you logs.”

[11:12] Felix Schneider: Fair. Today we have per-request metering and internal analytics. We can share exports and build you a report. A first-class customer-facing dashboard is something we’re working toward, but we’re not promising it as a product feature for day one. Internally, we’re investing heavily in a unit economics view because it drives optimization.

[11:33] Maya Patel: Okay, but for us, even a CSV export is fine if it’s correct and consistent.

[11:38] Elena Rios: Yeah, as long as it’s not a custom one-off every month.

[11:42] Felix Schneider: Understood. The direction we can take is: (1) define the metric clearly, (2) ensure the dimensions exist and aren’t changing, and (3) provide a stable API or scheduled export.

[11:56] Allison Grant: Also, we need to be careful about cardinality. Like, if you ask for cost by customer id, that can explode the metric system. But by model/region/tier is usually safe.

[12:09] Jon Kim: Totally. We don’t need per request on a dashboard. We need rollups.

[12:13] Maya Patel: For customer reporting we might need per workspace, but that’s later.

[12:18] Felix Schneider: Great.

[12:20] Felix Schneider: So, let’s define the drilldowns you care about. You said model, region. What about “customer tier” or plan type.

[12:28] Elena Rios: Eventually. Like self-serve vs enterprise plan. For now, just total and by region. But if you support dedicated vs shared, we’d need to separate that.

[12:40] Felix Schneider: Yes. Typically you’d want hosted vs dedicated vs private, because the cost model is different.

[12:46] Jon Kim: We won’t do private. Dedicated maybe later.

[12:50] Felix Schneider: Cool.

[12:52] Maya Patel: Another ask is “top drivers.” Like, can you show “cache hit rate,” “batching,” average output length, streaming vs non-streaming. Those are the levers we can influence.

[13:06] Allison Grant: That’s aligned with how we look at it. The unit cost number alone doesn’t help you debug.

[13:12] Jon Kim: Exactly.

[13:14] Felix Schneider: Okay, I’m going to ask a few qualification questions. Timeline: when do you need this in place.

[13:20] Maya Patel: We want to make a decision this quarter. Our pricing change is planned for end of Q1.

[13:26] Elena Rios: For reporting, I’d like something in February so we can model pricing.

[13:33] Felix Schneider: Got it. Volume: what’s your current monthly token usage roughly.

[13:38] Maya Patel: We’re around 8 to 12 billion tokens a month total across vendors. Output maybe 3 to 4 billion? It’s growing.

[13:49] Felix Schneider: That’s meaningful.

[13:51] Jon Kim: Peak QPS is spiky. When customers run backfills, it’s a lot. Then quiet.

[13:58] Allison Grant: That will impact batching. If you’re spiky, we can still batch, but it depends on your concurrency and latency SLO.

[14:07] Jon Kim: Our latency target is like 1.5 seconds to first token for chat, and total under 10 seconds typically.

[14:15] Felix Schneider: Okay.

[14:17] Maya Patel: Another thing: our customers compare us to Groq demos and they’re like “why isn’t it instant.” So we’re trying to keep latency down.

[14:26] Felix Schneider: Yep, Groq is in the mix a lot. The tradeoff is model selection and context length. But anyway.

[14:34] Felix Schneider: So, cost reporting. What format do you want? A dashboard, an API, a scheduled email, what’s easiest.

[14:42] Elena Rios: If it’s an API, that’s ideal. If not, even a daily export to S3 would be fine. We can ingest.

[14:50] Jon Kim: Yeah we have our own warehouse.

[14:52] Allison Grant: Makes sense.

[14:55] Felix Schneider: Okay. Let me propose an initial approach: we give you hourly or daily aggregates with dimensions: model_id, model_version, region, streaming flag. Maybe also quant_profile if relevant. And metrics: output_tokens, input_tokens, total_cost_usd, and then derived cost_per_1m_output_tokens.

[15:18] Elena Rios: That’s exactly it.

[15:20] Maya Patel: And maybe “request count” so we can see volume.

[15:23] Felix Schneider: Yes, request_count.

[15:26] Jon Kim: Also tool-calling vs not. Because our agent workflows call tools.

[15:31] Allison Grant: Tool calling is basically a route/type dimension. We can discuss, but we should be cautious with cardinality. “request_type=tool_call” is okay; “tool_name=…” can explode.

[15:44] Jon Kim: Yeah, just a boolean or type is fine.

[15:48] Felix Schneider: Good.

[15:50] Maya Patel: Can you talk about how you compute cost? Like, where does “cost” come from.

[15:55] Felix Schneider: For hosted, we can attribute cost based on compute usage and an internal rate card per region/hardware class. For dedicated, it’s based on reserved spend allocated over time. The important piece is: we can provide a “blended cost” definition that’s consistent, but it’s not the same as your invoice line items unless we reconcile.

[16:17] Elena Rios: Right. We need a reconciliation story.

[16:20] Felix Schneider: Exactly. Like: “sum of allocated costs across regions equals total infra cost for that period,” with known differences: credits, support fees, rounding, and so on.

[16:33] Elena Rios: Also taxes, maybe.

[16:35] Felix Schneider: Yeah.

[16:37] Allison Grant: One note: if you use multiple models with different hardware, the cost model should reflect that. If one model is on H100 and another is on A10, you can’t just average.

[16:49] Jon Kim: Of course.

[16:51] Maya Patel: Can we get cost by model and by region in the same report? Like a pivot.

[16:56] Felix Schneider: Yes. That’s the intent: group by model, region.

[17:00] Jon Kim: Okay.

[17:02] Felix Schneider: Let’s talk about region naming. When you say eu-west, do you mean Ireland specifically, or any EU.

[17:08] Maya Patel: Mostly Ireland, but “EU” is fine as long as it’s consistent. We might want Germany later.

[17:15] Felix Schneider: Got it.

[17:16] Jon Kim: Also we use AWS region strings internally. So eu-west-1, us-east-1. If you have something else, we need mapping.

[17:26] Allison Grant: We can provide normalized region. If our internal is different, we’ll map to something like “aws:eu-west-1” or “gcp:europe-west4.” We can agree on canonical strings.

[17:40] Jon Kim: Perfect.

[17:42] Maya Patel: Another pain we had: vendors sometimes show “model name” that changes. Like “Llama 70B Turbo” and then it’s actually a different checkpoint. We want stable identifiers.

[17:55] Felix Schneider: Yeah. We separate display name and the internal id. The dashboard would use stable internal id, and we can show a friendly alias.

[18:04] Jon Kim: Great.

[18:06] Felix Schneider: Okay. Let’s check on competitors you’ve tried. You said Together. Any Bedrock.

[18:12] Jon Kim: We looked at Bedrock but it’s hard to get consistent performance. Also cost reporting is not super friendly.

[18:20] Maya Patel: And some of our customers don’t like AWS-specific stuff.

[18:25] Felix Schneider: Understood.

[18:27] Allison Grant: For the internal “why did cost change,” besides caching and batching, another factor is average output length. If your users start asking for longer answers, output tokens go up and also the cost per request goes up. But cost per output token might stay stable. So we’d want both.

[18:47] Maya Patel: That’s why we like cost per output token. It normalizes.

[18:51] Elena Rios: But also, if output length changes, our revenue changes, because we price on output. So normalizing makes sense.

[18:59] Jon Kim: But for long-context, the normalization hides input cost.

[19:03] Allison Grant: Exactly.

[19:04] Felix Schneider: So maybe you’ll want a secondary metric: “$/1M total tokens” and “$/request,” depending on workload.

[19:11] Elena Rios: Yeah we can handle multiple, but let’s start with output.

[19:16] Felix Schneider: Cool.

[19:18] Maya Patel: So the real question: can you commit to providing this data if we move traffic.

[19:23] Felix Schneider: We can commit to providing token metering and the required dimensions. For the blended cost number, we can provide it as an internal metric export with a defined methodology. I want to be careful to not overpromise a polished UI, but the data can be there.

[19:41] Elena Rios: As long as there’s a definition doc.

[19:43] Felix Schneider: Yes.

[19:45] Jon Kim: And streaming parity.

[19:47] Allison Grant: We’ll validate streaming parity. If we find a gap, we’ll be transparent and fix it. Practically we’d recommend a validation period where you compare your client-side tokenization with what we report.

[20:03] Jon Kim: Good.

[20:05] Maya Patel: Can you also comment on how you handle retries. Because that can inflate tokens.

[20:10] Felix Schneider: Yes, retries are a big driver. We can mark requests as retry attempts and you can include/exclude. For cost, the compute is real, so you probably want it included, but for “quality regression” you might want to isolate.

[20:27] Maya Patel: Makes sense.

[20:30] Elena Rios: Also, credits. Sometimes vendors give credits that show up weird.

[20:34] Felix Schneider: Right. The blended cost metric usually excludes promotional credits and focuses on underlying infra cost, but your vendor invoice includes credits. So the reconciliation view needs to show both, or at least label.

[20:50] Elena Rios: Okay.

[20:52] Jon Kim: On the quantization profile, do you have a standard set of values? Because we’ve seen “int8”, “int8-kv”, “awq”, etc. It’s messy.

[21:02] Allison Grant: We enforce an allowlist. Otherwise you get high-cardinality explosions. But yes, we can agree on canonical values like “fp16”, “int8”, “int4_awq” etc.

[21:15] Jon Kim: Great.

[21:17] Felix Schneider: Let’s do a quick recap of what we think you need:
- Metric: blended $ per 1M output tokens
- Drilldowns: model, model version, region
- Supporting signals: cache hit rate, batching utilization, average output length, streaming vs non-streaming
- Requirements: stable definitions, reconciliation vs invoice, streaming token parity
Sound right?

[21:42] Maya Patel: Yes.

[21:43] Elena Rios: Yes.

[21:45] Jon Kim: Yes.

[21:47] Felix Schneider: Okay. And next steps: can we get your traffic profile? Like a histogram of input/output tokens and percent streaming and QPS peaks.

[21:56] Jon Kim: Yes, I can send that.

[21:58] Maya Patel: We can also share a couple representative workflows.

[22:02] Felix Schneider: Great.

[22:04] Allison Grant: And I’ll follow up with what telemetry dimensions are available today and any caveats. Also, if you want, we can draft the schema for the daily aggregates.

[22:15] Elena Rios: That would be helpful. Like literally column names.

[22:18] Felix Schneider: Cool.

[22:20] Maya Patel: Timing-wise, can we do a technical session next week.

[22:24] Felix Schneider: Yep. We can do a 60-min technical deep dive. We’ll bring someone from runtime if needed, but maybe not required.

[22:33] Jon Kim: I’d love that. Especially around batching/caching and how it affects latency.

[22:39] Felix Schneider: Perfect.

[22:41] (crosstalk)

[22:42] Elena Rios: Sorry one more: will we be able to export by week and by month. Finance likes month.

[22:47] Felix Schneider: Yes. If we provide daily aggregates, you can roll up to week/month. Also note timezone boundaries can cause confusion. We usually standardize to UTC but finance sometimes wants Pacific or month-close.

[23:03] Elena Rios: We want month-close in Pacific ideally.

[23:06] Felix Schneider: Okay we can discuss. At minimum we’ll label the timezone.

[23:12] Maya Patel: Great.

[23:14] Felix Schneider: Any other questions before we wrap.

[23:17] Jon Kim: Not now.

[23:18] Elena Rios: I’m good.

[23:20] Maya Patel: We’re good. Thanks.

[23:22] Felix Schneider: Awesome. We’ll send follow-up with the sample report format and schedule the deep dive.

[23:28] Allison Grant: Thanks everyone.

[23:30] Call ends / recording stops

(Recording continued with silence; Fireflies trimmed)
